title: Revealing Entanglement-Growth Mechanisms through the Magic Barrier
authors: Lv Zhang, Shi-Xin Zhang, Heng Fan, Shuo Liu
abstract: Quantum entanglement and magic are complementary resources underlying quantum computational advantage, yet their dynamical relation in many-body systems remains poorly understood. In this Letter, we show that the mechanism of bipartite entanglement growth is encoded in the relative timescale between the entropy-growth-rate peak and the magic barrier, defined as the transient peak of the anti-flatness of the entanglement spectrum. When entanglement is locally built, the same microscopic process increases the entropy and reshapes the Schmidt spectrum, so the magic-barrier peak occurs in the time window of maximal entropy growth. When entanglement is mainly transported or redistributed, entropy can grow before appreciable spectral non-flatness is generated, naturally separating the two peak times. We demonstrate this distinction in the random-field XXZ chain: the two peaks remain strongly correlated in the thermal regime, while their separation grows systematically across the thermal--MBL crossover. We further validate this theoretical framework by employing Bell-pair initial states alongside a tunable SWAP--Haar random circuit. Our results reveal an intrinsic dynamical connection between entanglement and magic, establishing the magic barrier as a powerful spectral diagnostic of how quantum information is generated, transported, and reshaped.
summary: The paper introduces the concept of 'magic barrier' anti-flatness as a diagnostic tool to probe how entanglement grows dynamically. By analyzing the time separation between this spectral feature and the peak entropy growth rate, the authors successfully distinguish between mechanisms where entanglement is locally built versus those where it is merely transported or redistributed in many-body systems.
main_problem: The study aims to elucidate the dynamical relationship between bipartite entanglement growth and quantum magic (nonstabilizerness) in complex many-body systems.
main_result: The relative timescale separation ($\Delta t_{	ext{sep}}$) between the peak of entropy growth rate and the 'magic barrier' peak serves as a diagnostic tool, distinguishing between local build mechanisms and entanglement transport/redistribution processes.
method: Theoretical analysis using quench dynamics simulations on random-field spin chains and controlled benchmarking with tunable random quantum circuits.
model_or_system: The primary model is the random-field XXZ chain, which is studied across a crossover from thermal to Many-Body Localized (MBL) regimes. Benchmarking uses random circuits simulating local building versus pure transport dynamics.
key_observables: Bipartite von Neumann entropy ($S_A$), its growth rate ($\dot{S}_A(t)$), and the anti-flatness of the entanglement spectrum ($F_A(t)$).
important_parameters: Disorder strength ($W$) controlling the thermal-MBL crossover, and a tunable parameter ($r$ or $p$) controlling the balance between local building (Haar gates) and transport (SWAP gates).
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes that entanglement growth can be decomposed into distinct mechanisms: local generation ('build') versus non-local movement ('transport').
figures_summary: Figures illustrate how $\dot{S}_A(t)$ and $F_A(t)$ peak times separate ($\Delta t_{	ext{sep}}$ increases) as disorder grows or when transport dominates, contrasting with the strong correlation seen in local build scenarios.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the theoretical link between entanglement and magic via $\Delta t_{	ext{sep}}$, applies this diagnostic to the random-field XXZ chain across different disorder regimes, and validates the framework using controlled random circuit simulations that tune the relative contributions of building versus transporting quantum information.
why_interesting: This work provides a powerful spectral diagnostic tool ($\Delta t_{	ext{sep}}$) to distinguish fundamental physical processes (local scrambling vs. global transport) in interacting quantum many-body systems, which is highly relevant for understanding thermalization and localization dynamics.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. Schematic of build- and transport-dominated entan- glement growth. (a) Transport redistributes pre-existing en- tanglement across the cut and can increase SA through an approximately flat Schmidt block, producing little or no anti- flatness. Local build processes instead split Schmidt sectors nonuniformly, generating FA while increasing SA. (b) Conse- quently, transport-dominated dynamics can separate the peak of ˙SA from the magic-barrier peak of FA, whereas build- dominated dynamics keeps the two peaks in the same time window.

FIG. 2. Dynamics of anti-flatness and entropy growth in the random-field XXZ chain. The half-chain anti-flatness FA (green) and entropy-growth rate ˙SA (purple) are shown for W = 1 [(a),(c)] and W = 20 [(b),(d)] at system size L = 14. The upper row uses random product initial states in the half-filling sector, while the middle row uses Bell-pair initial states with no Bell pair crossing either half-chain bipartition boundary. Vertical dashed lines mark the corresponding peak positions t∗ F and t∗ ˙S. All data are averaged over at least 1500 disorder realizations. (e) Peak separation ∆tsep = t∗ F −t∗ ˙S versus disorder strength W for product and Bell-pair initial states.

FIG. 3. Random-circuit benchmark initialized from Bell pairs. At each elementary update, a randomly chosen nearest- neighbor bond is acted on by a SWAP gate with probability 1 −r or by a Haar random two-qubit gate with probability r. The panels show SA(t), ˙SA(t), FA(t), and the peak sep- aration ∆tsep for L = 16. Increasing the Haar-gate fraction strengthens local build processes and pulls the magic-barrier peak toward the early entropy-growth window, thereby reduc- ing ∆tsep.
